title: After My Clinical Clerkship at Duke University
paragraphs: From April to June 2007, a period of three months, I was allowed to study at Duke University in North Carolina, in the United States. These three months were a time for learning about another country through the various differences and commonalities not only in medicine but also in culture, and for rediscovering my home country. In a completely new environment where each step of every day required challenges and efforts large and small, I was able to spend very fresh and enjoyable days because of that.

During the three months, I trained in pediatric infectious diseases, pediatric immunology and allergy, and pediatric endocrinology. I trained only at the university hospital and only in pediatrics, but the decisive difference I felt from the Japanese medical setting was "room in time." First, there are many doctors relative to the number of patients, from students, residents and fellows to attendings, and each level of doctor takes in information by receiving the presentation from the doctor at the level below and then examines the same patient. Also, cooperation between departments is close, and doctors from several departments come to round on a single inpatient, so many doctors' eyes are on each inpatient. However, the doctor of each department mainly looks at the part of the patient's problems related to his or her own specialty. And outpatient consultations are basically fully by appointment. For these reasons, I felt that the workload of one doctor has "room in time" compared with Japan. The benefits of that "room" seemed to me to be "EBM" and "consideration for patients." As for "EBM," whether in daily conferences or in the middle of rounds, seeing them use the computers found all over the ward to search the literature on the management and treatment of similar cases, I was convinced that this is what practising EBM means. As a result of such a search, they would go straight into a heated discussion about treatment policy, and there were times when everyone stood together in front of a patient's room and talked passionately for as long as two hours. Lectures and study sessions were also held frequently, and an environment was in place for further improving knowledge and skills in parallel with daily work. At these meetings, it was impressive that everyone listened to the presentations intently, fired off questions one after another, and nobody was dozing off, and the atmosphere was very lively and proactive. As for "consideration for patients," I was impressed by the length of time spent on examining or making rounds of a single patient (sometimes 30 minutes to an hour), by how during that long time they gave thorough explanations about the disease, treatment, side effects, prognosis and daily life, listened to questions, and discussed together the various options for treatment. Perhaps because enough time is taken to face patients in this way, it was impressive that there were times when they chatted and laughed, and patients naturally asked the doctors questions. Also, there are many kinds of medical professionals, and psychological support for patients was well organised as a system, including counselling by several kinds of counsellors and clergy (such as pastors). How can such "EBM" and "consideration for patients" be practised in Japan? Unless there is a policy to increase the number of doctors relative to the number of patients, we may have no choice but to continue to depend on the efforts of individual doctors. What is absolutely common to Japanese and American doctors, and what I am proud of as someone who aspired to this path, is that doctors in both countries strive to do their best in their respective environments.

During the clerkship, the doctors at Duke University were extremely kind to me. They gave mini-lectures during outpatient practice and rounds, listened carefully to my presentations even though my language was halting and gave feedback, and once I was used to the language, they let me do the preliminary interviews in the outpatient clinic every day. I was also greatly helped by the generosity and open-mindedness of the many patients and families who talked to a dubious foreigner like me who could barely speak the language, let me examine them, and in the end even encouraged me. I was also able to get to know not only American friends but also international students and researchers who had gathered from all over the world, and talking about each other's medical education and healthcare systems, and even about culture and customs, I felt both the pleasure of learning new perspectives and ways of thinking and the good fortune and importance of having a common language. I came across interesting surprises here and there, such as the words of a student from Taiwan, "In Japanese medical schools, classes are in Japanese, not English? That means doing the work twice, and it's behind the times," and the story of a Swiss student about his two years of military service. Culturally, I also got a glimpse of the reality of the United States, called the "melting pot," in that many of the patients at Duke University were neatly dressed white people, that when they were not, they were patients with rare diseases that were the subject of research or with specified diseases whose medical costs are exempted, and that the hospital cleaning staff were mostly African Americans and Latin Americans. It was also an interesting fact that African Americans and Latin Americans were on the whole kinder to me, an Asian, than Caucasians or the people who looked Asian only in appearance, probably second- or third-generation residents in the United States.

These three months passed in the blink of an eye, yet they became a period more full of discoveries and surprises than any three months I had had before. Finally, I am deeply grateful to the doctors and academic affairs staff of the International Exchange Office of Nagoya University and the people at Duke University who gave me such a valuable and wonderful opportunity. Thank you very much.
